title: Plant Breeding
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Botany/Plant Science Plant Breeding curriculum building on 200/300L genetics and plant physiology: modes of reproduction, breeding methods for self- and cross-pollinated crops, heterosis and hybrid seed production, mutation and polyploidy breeding, germplasm resources, molecular/marker-assisted breeding, and breeding for resistance and quality traits.

questions.question: Which of the following is a self-pollinated crop, requiring breeding methods (e.g. pedigree, bulk) suited to largely homozygous populations?
options: Maize
Rice
Pearl millet
Sugar beet
questions.correct_answer: Rice
questions.explanation: Rice is predominantly self-pollinated (autogamous), producing highly homozygous inbred lines, unlike cross-pollinated crops such as maize and pearl millet which are naturally outbred.

questions.question: Apomixis in plant breeding refers to:
options: Sexual reproduction involving fusion of gametes
Asexual reproduction through seed, producing offspring genetically identical to the maternal parent without fertilisation
Artificial cross-pollination by hand
The process of doubling chromosome number using colchicine
questions.correct_answer: Asexual reproduction through seed, producing offspring genetically identical to the maternal parent without fertilisation
questions.explanation: Apomixis is a form of asexual (agamic) reproduction in which seeds are formed without meiosis and fertilisation, producing progeny that are genetic clones of the mother plant -- of great interest for fixing hybrid vigour.

questions.question: The pure line theory, formulated by Wilhelm Johannsen, established that within a pure line (derived from a single self-pollinated homozygous plant):
options: Further selection is effective in changing the population's genetic mean
Selection is ineffective in altering the genotype because all individuals are genetically identical, and observed variation is purely environmental
All individuals are heterozygous
Mutation rate is zero
questions.correct_answer: Selection is ineffective in altering the genotype because all individuals are genetically identical, and observed variation is purely environmental
questions.explanation: Johannsen's pure line theory showed that within a genetically homozygous pure line, phenotypic variation is entirely environmental, so selection within the pure line cannot shift the population's genetic mean; selection is only effective among pure lines, not within one.

questions.question: In the pedigree method of breeding self-pollinated crops, a key feature is that:
options: No record of ancestry is kept from generation to generation
Individual plant selection is practised in segregating generations (from F2 onward) with detailed records of ancestry maintained
Selection is delayed until the F10 generation
It is used exclusively for hybrid seed production in cross-pollinated crops
questions.correct_answer: Individual plant selection is practised in segregating generations (from F2 onward) with detailed records of ancestry maintained
questions.explanation: The pedigree method involves selecting individual plants in each segregating generation starting from F2, with careful pedigree records kept to track the ancestry and performance of each selected line.

questions.question: The bulk population method of breeding differs from the pedigree method primarily in that:
options: Selection is delayed until later generations (often F5-F6) when the population has become largely homozygous, and individual selection/pedigree records are not maintained in early generations
Selection begins immediately in the F1 generation
It can only be applied to cross-pollinated crops
It requires continuous backcrossing to a recurrent parent
questions.correct_answer: Selection is delayed until later generations (often F5-F6) when the population has become largely homozygous, and individual selection/pedigree records are not maintained in early generations
questions.explanation: In the bulk method, segregating generations are grown in bulk (harvested and advanced as a mixed population) without individual selection or pedigree records until the population reaches near-homozygosity, allowing natural selection to act.

questions.question: The backcross breeding method is most appropriate for:
options: Combining many desirable traits from several unrelated parents simultaneously
Transferring one or a few simply inherited traits (e.g. disease resistance) from a donor parent into an otherwise well-adapted recurrent parent variety
Developing entirely new genotypes with no resemblance to either parent
Producing hybrid vigour in a single generation
questions.correct_answer: Transferring one or a few simply inherited traits (e.g. disease resistance) from a donor parent into an otherwise well-adapted recurrent parent variety
questions.explanation: Backcrossing repeatedly crosses progeny to the recurrent (adapted) parent while selecting for the trait of interest from the donor parent, efficiently transferring simply inherited traits while recovering the recurrent parent's genome.

questions.question: In a backcross breeding programme, after 'n' backcrosses to the recurrent parent, the expected proportion of the recurrent parent genome recovered in the progeny is approximately:
options: 100% after just one backcross
questions.explanation: The expected recurrent parent genome recovery after n backcrosses is 1 - (1/2)^(n+1); e.g. after BC1 it is about 75%, after BC5 about 98.4%, approaching but never fully reaching 100%.

questions.question: Heterosis (hybrid vigour) refers to the phenomenon in which:
options: The F1 hybrid performs inferior to both parents
The F1 hybrid exhibits superior performance (e.g. yield, vigour) compared to the mean or better parent
Inbreeding increases vigour indefinitely
Hybrids are always sterile
questions.correct_answer: The F1 hybrid exhibits superior performance (e.g. yield, vigour) compared to the mean or better parent
questions.explanation: Heterosis is the superiority of the F1 hybrid over its parents in traits such as yield, vigour, or stress tolerance, commonly exploited commercially in crops like maize.

questions.question: The dominance hypothesis is one proposed genetic explanation for heterosis. It attributes hybrid vigour to:
options: The masking of deleterious recessive alleles from one parent by dominant favourable alleles from the other parent, concentrated in the heterozygous F1
Overdominance at every single locus without exception
Complete absence of gene interaction
Increased mutation rate in the hybrid
questions.correct_answer: The masking of deleterious recessive alleles from one parent by dominant favourable alleles from the other parent, concentrated in the heterozygous F1
questions.explanation: The dominance hypothesis explains heterosis as resulting from linked dominant favourable alleles from both parents complementing each other in the F1, masking the expression of deleterious recessive alleles carried by either parent.

questions.question: Cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS) is exploited commercially in hybrid seed production mainly to:
options: Increase the plant's photosynthetic rate
Avoid the need for labour-intensive manual emasculation when producing hybrid seed on a large scale
Make the plant resistant to herbicides
Induce polyploidy in the seed parent
questions.correct_answer: Avoid the need for labour-intensive manual emasculation when producing hybrid seed on a large scale
questions.explanation: CMS lines are pollen-sterile due to cytoplasmic (mitochondrial) genes, so they cannot self-pollinate; this eliminates the need for hand emasculation of the female parent in large-scale hybrid seed production, such as for maize, sorghum, and pearl millet.

questions.question: In a cytoplasmic-genetic male sterility (CMS) hybrid seed production system, a 'restorer line' is used to:
options: Maintain male sterility in the seed parent
Carry a dominant fertility-restorer (Rf) nuclear gene that restores pollen fertility in the F1 hybrid grown by farmers
Serve as the female parent exclusively
Prevent cross-pollination entirely
questions.correct_answer: Carry a dominant fertility-restorer (Rf) nuclear gene that restores pollen fertility in the F1 hybrid grown by farmers
questions.explanation: The restorer line carries dominant Rf nuclear genes that restore normal pollen fertility when crossed onto a CMS line, so the resulting F1 hybrid seed sold to farmers is fertile and can set seed/grain normally.

questions.question: General combining ability (GCA) of an inbred line refers to:
options: Its average performance in hybrid combination across a series of crosses with other lines
The performance of a specific single cross only
Its performance when self-pollinated
Its resistance to a specific pathogen strain
questions.correct_answer: Its average performance in hybrid combination across a series of crosses with other lines
questions.explanation: GCA is the average performance of a line in a series of hybrid combinations (crosses), largely attributed to additive gene action, as distinguished from specific combining ability (SCA) which reflects the performance of a particular cross.

questions.question: Specific combining ability (SCA) is primarily attributed to which type of gene action?
options: Purely additive gene action
Non-additive gene action, particularly dominance and epistasis
Cytoplasmic inheritance only
Environmental variance only
questions.correct_answer: Non-additive gene action, particularly dominance and epistasis
questions.explanation: SCA reflects the deviation of a specific cross's performance from what would be predicted by the GCA of its parents, and is largely due to non-additive gene effects (dominance and epistasis).

questions.question: Inbreeding depression, commonly observed when normally cross-pollinated crops such as maize are self-pollinated, is characterised by:
options: An increase in vigour and yield with successive generations of selfing
A progressive decline in vigour, yield, and fertility as heterozygosity decreases and deleterious recessive alleles become homozygous
No change in the population at all
Complete sterility after a single generation of selfing
questions.correct_answer: A progressive decline in vigour, yield, and fertility as heterozygosity decreases and deleterious recessive alleles become homozygous
questions.explanation: Inbreeding depression results from increased homozygosity exposing deleterious recessive alleles, causing reduced vigour and yield in normally outcrossing species -- the flip side of heterosis seen when inbred lines are subsequently hybridised.

questions.question: Recurrent selection is a breeding scheme mainly used for improving cross-pollinated (outbreeding) crops. Its main objective is to:
options: Fix a single homozygous line as quickly as possible
Gradually increase the frequency of favourable alleles in a population through repeated cycles of selection and intermating, while maintaining genetic variability
Eliminate all genetic variation in one generation
Only be used for vegetatively propagated crops
questions.correct_answer: Gradually increase the frequency of favourable alleles in a population through repeated cycles of selection and intermating, while maintaining genetic variability
questions.explanation: Recurrent selection cycles selection of superior individuals with subsequent intermating among them, progressively improving population mean performance while preserving sufficient genetic variability for continued gains.

questions.question: A synthetic variety in plant breeding is developed by:
options: Intercrossing a number of genotypes with good combining ability, and the resulting population can be maintained by farmers through open pollination for several generations
Doubling the chromosome number of a diploid species
Cloning a single elite plant vegetatively
Mutagenic treatment of seeds with gamma radiation
questions.correct_answer: Intercrossing a number of genotypes with good combining ability, and the resulting population can be maintained by farmers through open pollination for several generations
questions.explanation: A synthetic variety is produced by intermating several selected lines/clones with good general combining ability; unlike a single-cross hybrid, farmers can save and replant synthetic seed for a few generations with only gradual loss of vigour.

questions.question: Mutation breeding, using agents such as gamma rays, X-rays, or chemical mutagens like ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS), is primarily employed to:
options: Transfer entire chromosomes from a wild relative
Induce novel genetic variation for traits not available in existing germplasm, which can then be selected and incorporated into breeding programmes
Guarantee that all resulting mutants are beneficial
Eliminate the need for any subsequent selection
questions.correct_answer: Induce novel genetic variation for traits not available in existing germplasm, which can then be selected and incorporated into breeding programmes
questions.explanation: Mutation breeding uses physical or chemical mutagens to induce random mutations, creating new genetic variability (most mutations are neutral or deleterious, but rare useful mutants, e.g. for plant height or disease resistance, can be selected).

questions.question: Colchicine is widely used in plant breeding, particularly in polyploidy breeding, because it:
options: Inhibits spindle fibre formation during mitosis, preventing chromosome separation and resulting in chromosome doubling
Induces point mutations in DNA bases
Acts as a selective herbicide
Promotes cross-pollination in self-pollinated crops
questions.correct_answer: Inhibits spindle fibre formation during mitosis, preventing chromosome separation and resulting in chromosome doubling
questions.explanation: Colchicine disrupts microtubule/spindle formation during cell division, so replicated chromosomes fail to separate into daughter cells, doubling the chromosome number -- widely used to convert diploids to tetraploids or to restore fertility in wide hybrids.

questions.question: An allopolyploid, such as bread wheat (Triticum aestivum, hexaploid), arises from:
options: Doubling of the chromosome number of a single species (autopolyploidy)
Chromosome doubling following hybridisation between two or more different species, combining and doubling their distinct genomes
Simple mitotic division without any hybridisation
Loss of an entire chromosome set
questions.correct_answer: Chromosome doubling following hybridisation between two or more different species, combining and doubling their distinct genomes
questions.explanation: Allopolyploids result from interspecific hybridisation followed by chromosome doubling, combining complete diploid genome sets from different parental species; bread wheat is a classic hexaploid allopolyploid derived from three ancestral grass genomes.

questions.question: Wide (distant) hybridisation, crossing genetically distant species or genera, often results in weak or aborted hybrid embryos. Which technique is commonly used to rescue such crosses?
options: Grafting
Embryo culture (embryo rescue)
Seed dormancy breaking with cold stratification only
Vernalisation
questions.correct_answer: Embryo culture (embryo rescue)
questions.explanation: Embryo rescue involves excising immature or weak hybrid embryos from wide crosses and culturing them in vitro on nutrient media, bypassing endosperm failure or other barriers that would otherwise abort the embryo in planta.

questions.question: Germplasm collections held in seed genebanks are primarily important to plant breeders because they:
options: Guarantee immediate release of new varieties without further testing
Preserve genetic diversity, including landraces and wild relatives, as a reservoir of useful alleles for future breeding needs
Eliminate the need for field trials
Are used only for ornamental purposes
questions.correct_answer: Preserve genetic diversity, including landraces and wild relatives, as a reservoir of useful alleles for future breeding needs
questions.explanation: Germplasm banks conserve the genetic diversity of crop landraces, wild relatives, and breeding lines, serving as a critical resource of alleles (e.g. for disease resistance, stress tolerance) that breeders can draw upon.

questions.question: Marker-assisted selection (MAS) in modern plant breeding uses molecular markers primarily to:
options: Directly alter the plant's DNA sequence
Track and select for genomic regions linked to a desired trait, without needing to phenotype the trait directly in every generation
Replace the need for any phenotypic evaluation permanently
Only be applicable to traits controlled by a single visible morphological marker
questions.correct_answer: Track and select for genomic regions linked to a desired trait, without needing to phenotype the trait directly in every generation
questions.explanation: MAS uses DNA markers (e.g. SSRs, SNPs) tightly linked to genes/QTLs controlling a trait of interest, allowing breeders to select plants carrying the desired allele at the seedling stage without waiting for the trait to be expressed phenotypically.

questions.question: Quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping is used in plant breeding to:
options: Identify chromosomal regions associated with the variation in a quantitatively inherited (polygenic) trait, such as yield or drought tolerance
Study traits controlled by a single Mendelian gene only
Eliminate genetic recombination entirely
Directly measure protein content without genetics
questions.correct_answer: Identify chromosomal regions associated with the variation in a quantitatively inherited (polygenic) trait, such as yield or drought tolerance
questions.explanation: QTL mapping uses molecular markers and statistical linkage analysis to locate genomic regions contributing to variation in complex, polygenic quantitative traits like yield, plant height, or stress tolerance.

questions.question: Transgenic (genetically modified) crops such as Bt cotton incorporate a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis primarily to confer:
options: Herbicide tolerance
Resistance to specific insect pests through production of an insecticidal crystal (Cry) protein toxic to target larvae
Drought tolerance
Increased seed size only
questions.correct_answer: Resistance to specific insect pests through production of an insecticidal crystal (Cry) protein toxic to target larvae
questions.explanation: Bt crops express Cry (crystal) proteins from Bacillus thuringiensis that are toxic when ingested by specific lepidopteran or coleopteran insect pests, providing built-in insect resistance and reducing reliance on chemical insecticides.

questions.question: Breeding for horizontal (durable) disease resistance, as opposed to vertical (race-specific) resistance, is generally preferred by breeders in the long term because horizontal resistance:
options: Is controlled by a single major gene and is easily overcome by new pathogen races
Is typically polygenic, providing partial but more durable resistance against a broad range of pathogen races
Guarantees complete immunity against every pathogen
Cannot be combined with agronomic traits
questions.correct_answer: Is typically polygenic, providing partial but more durable resistance against a broad range of pathogen races
questions.explanation: Horizontal resistance, conferred by multiple genes with small additive effects, tends to be more durable because it is harder for a pathogen to overcome simultaneously, unlike single-gene (vertical) resistance which pathogens can defeat via a single mutation.

questions.question: The 'gene-for-gene' hypothesis, proposed by Flor from studies of flax rust, describes the relationship between:
options: A host resistance (R) gene and a corresponding pathogen avirulence (Avr) gene, whose interaction determines resistance or susceptibility
Two unrelated genes in the same host with no pathogen involvement
The number of chromosomes in a polyploid series
Cytoplasmic and nuclear male sterility genes only
questions.correct_answer: A host resistance (R) gene and a corresponding pathogen avirulence (Avr) gene, whose interaction determines resistance or susceptibility
questions.explanation: The gene-for-gene hypothesis proposes that for each host resistance gene, there is a corresponding pathogen avirulence gene; resistance occurs only when the specific R gene product recognises the specific Avr gene product, triggering a defence response.

questions.question: In breeding for abiotic stress tolerance such as drought, a commonly used indirect selection trait in cereals is:
options: Flower colour
Root system architecture and osmotic adjustment capacity
Seed coat thickness alone
Leaf shape only
questions.correct_answer: Root system architecture and osmotic adjustment capacity
questions.explanation: Deep, extensive root systems and the capacity for osmotic adjustment (accumulating solutes to maintain cell turgor under water deficit) are important physiological traits breeders select for or use as indirect indicators of drought tolerance.

questions.question: Before a newly developed crop variety can be officially released for commercial cultivation in most national systems (including Nigeria's National Variety Release Committee process), it must undergo:
options: No formal evaluation; any breeder line can be sold directly
Multi-locational performance trials to confirm Distinctness, Uniformity, and Stability (DUS) and superior performance over existing checks
Only a single season's trial at the breeder's home station
Certification is unnecessary if the variety is a hybrid
questions.correct_answer: Multi-locational performance trials to confirm Distinctness, Uniformity, and Stability (DUS) and superior performance over existing checks
questions.explanation: Formal variety release requires multi-locational, multi-year trials demonstrating the new variety's Distinctness, Uniformity and Stability (DUS) and its agronomic superiority over existing released check varieties, before national release and seed certification.

questions.question: Plant Breeders' Rights (PBR), a form of intellectual property protection, are granted to breeders primarily to:
options: Give the breeder exclusive commercial rights over propagation and sale of a new, distinct, uniform, and stable variety for a defined period
Prevent any farmer anywhere from ever growing the variety
Grant patent rights over the plant species as a whole, including all future varieties
Replace the need for variety registration
questions.correct_answer: Give the breeder exclusive commercial rights over propagation and sale of a new, distinct, uniform, and stable variety for a defined period
questions.explanation: Plant Breeders' Rights, as under UPOV-type frameworks, grant the breeder of a new, distinct, uniform, and stable variety exclusive rights to control its commercial propagation and marketing for a set number of years, incentivising investment in breeding.

questions.question: Tissue culture techniques such as anther/microspore culture are valuable in plant breeding mainly because they can be used to:
options: Produce haploid plants that, after chromosome doubling, yield completely homozygous (doubled haploid) lines in a single generation
Increase the natural rate of cross-pollination
Eliminate the need for any field evaluation
Convert a cross-pollinated crop into an apomictic one
questions.correct_answer: Produce haploid plants that, after chromosome doubling, yield completely homozygous (doubled haploid) lines in a single generation
questions.explanation: Anther or microspore culture regenerates haploid plantlets from pollen; doubling their chromosomes (e.g. with colchicine) produces fully homozygous doubled-haploid lines much faster than the 6-8 generations of selfing normally needed in pedigree breeding.

questions.question: In quantitative genetics, broad-sense heritability (H^2) of a trait is defined as:
options: The ratio of additive genetic variance to total phenotypic variance
The ratio of total genotypic variance to total phenotypic variance
The ratio of environmental variance to genotypic variance
Always equal to 1.0 for any trait
questions.correct_answer: The ratio of total genotypic variance to total phenotypic variance
questions.explanation: Broad-sense heritability (H^2 = VG/VP) is the proportion of total phenotypic variance attributable to all genetic causes (additive, dominance, and epistatic variance combined), as opposed to narrow-sense heritability which uses only additive variance.

questions.question: Narrow-sense heritability (h^2), the ratio of additive genetic variance to total phenotypic variance, is of particular importance to plant breeders because it:
options: Has no bearing on breeding progress
Predicts the response to selection, since only additive genetic effects are reliably transmitted from parent to offspring
Is always higher than broad-sense heritability
Only applies to asexually propagated crops
questions.correct_answer: Predicts the response to selection, since only additive genetic effects are reliably transmitted from parent to offspring
questions.explanation: Narrow-sense heritability estimates the additive genetic component that offspring reliably inherit from their parents, making it directly useful for predicting the expected genetic gain (response) from a given selection intensity.
